zh: 找两个不同下标使和为 target，等价于对每个位置 j，问它前面有没有值等于 target−nums[j] 的元素。先出现的那个下标就是 i，天然满足 i<j。
从左到右扫描，用哈希表记录已经扫描过的值到下标的映射。处理当前元素时先查询补数，再把自己放进表里，这样当前元素永远不会和自己配对，重复值也能正确找到另一个位置。
建空哈希表 seen。对 j=0..n−1：令 x=nums[j]，若 target−x 在 seen 中，输出 seen[target−x] 和 j 并结束；否则令 seen[x]=j。题目保证恰有一个合法无序下标对，所以一定会在某一步找到。
en: Finding two distinct indices whose values sum to target is the same as asking, for each position j, whether an earlier element equals target - nums[j]. The earlier index is i, so i < j holds automatically.

Scan from left to right with a hash map from values already seen to their indices. For the current element, look up its complement first and only then insert the element itself, so it never pairs with itself and duplicate values still find their other position.

Start with an empty map seen. For j = 0..n - 1, let x = nums[j]; if target - x is in seen, print seen[target - x] and j and stop; otherwise set seen[x] = j. The input guarantees exactly one valid unordered index pair, so some step always finds it.

explanationEn:
## Source and Clarifications by This Site

The body text of the fixed raw snapshot is cut off after "return", but the full constraints are preserved: 2≤n≤10, nums and target both in [-10,10], and "Only one valid answer exists". The explanations of both original examples state directly that nums[0]+nums[1]==target and return [0,1], showing that the indices of the two numbers must be returned, not the element values. The fixed version's three source implementations, in Python, Java and C++, all look up earlier indices before inserting the current index, consistently using two distinct indices. On that basis this site states that the unique solution means a unique unordered index pair and outputs the 0-based indices in ascending order i<j. This does not disguise the missing original text as complete original text, and it is not merely a format conversion.

Original example 1, [2,7,11,15] with target=9, contains 11 and 15, which violate the value range given in the raw text. The constraints are neither widened nor narrowed, and that example is not used in the official tests. The valid original example 2, [2,7] with target=9, is kept. The other public examples are supplements by this site. Repeated values are allowed, but the same index cannot be used twice: the two 3s in [3,3] sit at different positions and form one valid index pair; for [-3,0,3] with target=0, only 0 and 2 can be returned, never 1 and 1.

## Approach

Scan from left to right; the hash table records only the values of elements already scanned and their indices. When the current value is x, first check whether target−x has already appeared; if it has, output its index and the current index. Otherwise record the current element. The input guarantees a unique valid unordered index pair, so no return value needs to be defined for the no-solution or multiple-solution cases.

## Proof of Correctness

Before index j is processed, the table holds only indices strictly smaller than j. When the complement is found, the result is i<j with nums[i]+nums[j]=target, so the indices are distinct, the order is canonical and the sum is correct. Let the unique solution be (i,j) with i<j; when j is processed, the complement has already appeared. If that complement had another, different earlier index, it would form a second valid index pair, contradicting the uniqueness guarantee, so the recorded index must be i. The algorithm therefore always finds and returns the unique solution. Looking up before inserting ensures the current element can never be paired with itself.

## Complexity and Full Bounds

Expected time O(n), extra space O(n). The full ranges are n=2..10, with elements and target all in -10..10. The sum of two elements lies in [-20,20], but target is still limited to [-10,10]. Every test is filtered by an independent double loop over i<j to guarantee exactly one solution; the maximum length, the largest and smallest values, the target endpoints, repeated positive and negative values, repeated zeros, and answer indices 8/9 all have official test cases.
